title: How .45 Parabellum Bloodhound bridges two gaming worlds
summary: TOKYO, Japan — For Christopher “kiririn51” Ortiz, game director and co-founder of Sukeban Games, .45 Parabellum Bloodhound started with a battle system from the past. Sukeban Games is best known for…

blocks.text: TOKYO, Japan — For Christopher “kiririn51” Ortiz, game director and co-founder of Sukeban Games, .45 Parabellum Bloodhound started with a battle system from the past.
Sukeban Games is best known for VA-11 HALL-A, the cyberpunk bartender visual novel that established the studio and its narrative-driven approach.
With .45 Parabellum Bloodhound, the developers are stepping into something more action-oriented while trying to retain that storytelling focus.
Looking at the combat of Parasite Eve, Ortiz saw a way to bridge those two worlds.

“It kinda began looking at the Parasite Eve battle system. And I was like, oh, this is like the perfect bridge between a more action-oriented gameplay and more like the narrative side that we explored in VA-11 HALL-A,” said Ortiz in an interview with Tech INQ during Tokyo Game Show 2026.
.45 Parabellum Bloodhound follows Reila Mikazuchi, a former mercenary emerging from depression who attempts to rebuild her life by returning to the work she knows best.
Its “Active Time Action” system has players move and dodge in real time while waiting for an Action bar to fill before stopping time to plan their offense.
That ability to slow things down was particularly important for Ortiz as Sukeban Games ventured beyond the visual novel genre.
“People who play visual novels usually are not the type to play action games. So, like I said, it’s a perfect bridge for it,” said Ortiz.

Despite featuring damage numbers, upgrades and character customization, Ortiz is hesitant to simply call .45 Parabellum Bloodhound an action RPG.
“It’s not about making an action game, it’s not about making an RPG, it’s about giving players a certain atmosphere, a certain feel, by using video game language,” said Ortiz.
That includes giving players flexibility in how they build and play Reila.
“I want people to just explore every type of possible build in the game, with complete flexibility,” said Ortiz.
That freedom also reflects its protagonist. Ortiz describes Reila, a former mercenary and soldier, as someone who has learned to constantly adapt.
“She has to adapt to every situation all the time. Former mercenary, former soldier, she’s just trying to keep coming back to this life because she’s got nothing going on,” explained Ortiz.
Death gives players a chance to do the same. Returning to a checkpoint allows them to rethink their approach, from changing weapons to choosing different implants or spells.
